title: Jackson opens the case

facts.text: On 21 November 1945, the second day of the Nuremberg trial, Robert H. Jackson, chief of counsel for the United States, opened the prosecution's case before the International Military Tribunal.
Jackson was a sitting justice of the US Supreme Court. President Harry S. Truman had appointed him chief prosecutor, and he took a leave of absence from the Court to do it.

Before he spoke, the defendants entered their pleas. Hermann Goering tried to make a statement and was cut off by the presiding judge; Rudolf Hess simply said "No", which the court entered as not guilty. Every defendant present pleaded not guilty.
Jackson began: "The privilege of opening the first trial in history for crimes against the peace of the world imposes a grave responsibility."

Then came his most quoted line: "The wrongs which we seek to condemn and punish have been so calculated, so malignant, and so devastating, that civilization cannot tolerate their being ignored, because it cannot survive their being repeated."

He went on: "That four great nations, flushed with victory and stung with injury stay the hand of vengeance and voluntarily submit their captive enemies to the judgment of the law is one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason."
He said the case rested on the Nazis' own records and promised: "We will show you their own films. You will see their own conduct and hear their own voices."
He told the judges that the real complaining party at their bar was "Civilization", and he finished the whole address that same day, before the tribunal adjourned until the next morning.
The National Archives holds a sound recording of the opening of the speech in Jackson's own voice.
The trial ran until 1 October 1946. Jackson then went back to his seat on the Supreme Court.

declassified.fact: Jackson's absence cost the Supreme Court dearly. He missed the entire 1945 Term, and important cases that split four to four had to be carried over to the next one. Chief Justice Harlan Fiske Stone, who disliked judges taking outside jobs, privately likened the trials to a lynching party.

body:
Four victorious nations held their captive enemies. Robert H. Jackson stood up in Nuremberg to explain why they were getting a trial instead of vengeance.

21 November 1945. On the second day of the trial, the chief of counsel for the United States opened the prosecution's case. Jackson was a sitting justice of the US Supreme Court; Truman had appointed him, and he took leave from the Court to do it.

He began: "The privilege of opening the first trial in history for crimes against the peace of the world imposes a grave responsibility."

Then came the line people remember: "civilization cannot tolerate their being ignored, because it cannot survive their being repeated."

That four great nations would "stay the hand of vengeance" and submit their enemies to the law, he said, was "one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason."

The case would rest on the Nazis' own records. "We will show you their own films," he promised. He finished the whole address that day, and when the trial ended in October 1946 he went back to the Court.
